title: the first symbol of the scripture
hook: the first symbol of the scripture — one

segments.voice: Yesterday: seva. Your line was one quiet thing for someone. Today, the very first mark in the Sikh scripture. Day nine.

Most books start with a title, or once upon a time. The Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, starts with a symbol. You may have seen it without knowing: on a gold pendant, a dashboard, over a shop door, on a forearm. A Gurmukhi numeral with a sweeping curve flying off the top. Before any story, any rule, any song: this.
screen: `A LONG BOOK OF HYMNS.` → `THE FIRST THING ISN'T A WORD.` → `IT'S A SYMBOL.`

segments.voice: It's called Ik Onkar. It starts with a numeral: the digit one. Not the word, the number, the one you'd write on a price tag. That's Ik. Then Onkar, a very old sound for the divine, related to Om, which Nanak's Hindu neighbors chanted. And the curve, sweeping up and out, which some Sikhs read as a line with no end. Together: there is one. One God, one reality, one source behind everything. Why a numeral? One way Sikh teachers explain it: a word belongs to one language, and can be argued with. Everyone agrees on one. And notice what that one includes. On this path, the one isn't far off, looking down on creation. The hymns say it's in everything: in you, in the person across the street, in the river and the dust. So if there's one, nobody stands outside it. You can hear Guru Nanak's line from day six underneath: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. If there's one, the labels come second.
screen: `IK — THE NUMERAL ONE.` · `ONKAR — AN ANCIENT SOUND FOR GOD.` · `A NUMBER NOBODY CAN ARGUE WITH.` · `IF THERE'S ONE, NO ONE IS OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: Breathe, and notice yourself: your hands, your chest rising. Then notice something beyond you: a sound in the room, someone you love. Then hold both at once, and if you like, let one word ride out on the breath: one.
Ik Onkar. The numeral one, joined to an ancient sound for God: there is one, and it opens the whole scripture. Ninth word.
Your line: one. Same source, for you and for the person who annoys you most. That's day nine.

screen: `DAY 9 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "ONE CREATOR, TRUTH IS THE NAME."`

howItsDone: Ik Onkar opens the Guru Granth Sahib and begins the Mool Mantar, which Sikhs recite daily; the symbol is written, painted and worn as a reminder of the one God.

fork.setup: you're opening a long scripture of hymns. what goes first?
options: the story of how the world began.
a single mark that says: there is one.
fork.reveal: Ik Onkar stands at the head of everything: before any story, rule or song.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the numeral one (੧) joined to the letter for Onkar, with its open curve; one symbol, one character.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty religious symbol.
what it means: there is one: one God, one source, in everything, so no one stands outside it.
what a scholar hears: it's a numeral, not a word, fused with Onkar, a form related to Om. Sikh commentators stress the numeral: one, without a second.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Ik Onkar at the head of the Mool Mantar)
Guru Granth Sahib, passim (the one God present in all)

notes: Onkar described as 'related to Om'; some Sikh commentators resist linking it to Om. Confirm the phrasing.
The curve read as 'a line with no end' is a common devotional reading, framed as 'some Sikhs read'. Confirm.
Pronunciation of ੴ varies (ik oankar, ik onkar, ek oangkar). Confirm the guide.
